    1. One degree higher, by hand . Foundational, 11 points. Question 1 of 5.

    Foundational 11 pts

    Every formula in this lesson comes out of a single computation: multiply the complete factorization out, and compare what you get with the coefficients you started from. This question runs that computation at degree four, which is wide enough for the pattern to be visible and still short enough to write in full. Throughout, r1,r2,r3,r4r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4r1​,r2​,r3​,r4​ are the four roots of a quartic, listed as the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra supplies them.

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 3

      One polynomial, written two ways: a product of linear factors on one side, a row of coefficients on the other. Every formula here is what falls out of insisting that those two descriptions agree.

    2. Hint 2 of 3 · Part B

      The identity you proved has a leading coefficient of one on both sides, and the polynomial here does not. A single division repairs that, and it is the division every formula then carries.

    3. Hint 3 of 3 · Part C

      Ask which numbers the roots are being drawn from before deciding the list is empty. Real coefficients promise nothing about real roots, and the theorem this chapter opened with promises something quite different.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    The coefficient of x3x^3x3 is −(r1+r2+r3+r4)-(r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4)−(r1​+r2​+r3​+r4​), that of x2x^2x2 is r1r2+r1r3+r1r4+r2r3+r2r4+r3r4r_1r_2 + r_1r_3 + r_1r_4 + r_2r_3 + r_2r_4 + r_3r_4r1​r2​+r1​r3​+r1​r4​+r2​r3​+r2​r4​+r3​r4​, that of xxx is −(r1r2r3+r1r2r4+r1r3r4+r2r3r4)-(r_1r_2r_3 + r_1r_2r_4 + r_1r_3r_4 + r_2r_3r_4)−(r1​r2​r3​+r1​r2​r4​+r1​r3​r4​+r2​r3​r4​), and the constant term is r1r2r3r4r_1r_2r_3r_4r1​r2​r3​r4​. The six terms of the x2x^2x2 coefficient are the products of two different entries.

    • Abbreviating those four coefficients as −e1-e_1−e1​, e2e_2e2​, −e3-e_3−e3​ and e4e_4e4​ names exactly the same sums
    • The six terms of the x2x^2x2 coefficient written in any order name the same sum

    Part B

    e1=−a3a4e_1 = -\frac{a_3}{a_4}e1​=−a4​a3​​, e2=a2a4e_2 = \frac{a_2}{a_4}e2​=a4​a2​​, e3=−a1a4e_3 = -\frac{a_1}{a_4}e3​=−a4​a1​​, e4=a0a4e_4 = \frac{a_0}{a_4}e4​=a4​a0​​. Making both sides monic is the step; without it each value comes out a4a_4a4​ times the true one.

    • ek=(−1)ka4−ka4e_k = (-1)^k\frac{a_{4-k}}{a_4}ek​=(−1)ka4​a4−k​​ for k=1,2,3,4k = 1, 2, 3, 4k=1,2,3,4 is the same four formulas written as one
    • e2=+a2a4e_2 = +\frac{a_2}{a_4}e2​=+a4​a2​​ and e4=+a0a4e_4 = +\frac{a_0}{a_4}e4​=+a4​a0​​ with the plus signs written in name the same values

    Part C

    No real number is a root, so the real numbers offer no list to run the formulas on, and an empty list adds to 000 rather than to the 444 the coefficients demand. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra supplies 2i2i2i, −2i-2i−2i, 2+3i2 + 3i2+3i, 2−3i2 - 3i2−3i, two conjugate pairs, and that list gives e1=4e_1 = 4e1​=4 and e4=52e_4 = 52e4​=52.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Multiply the given cubic by (x−r4)(x - r_4)(x−r4​) and distribute. The xxx reproduces the cubic one degree higher, and the −r4-r_4−r4​ multiplies every term of the cubic by −r4-r_4−r4​. Then collect like powers, one power at a time.

    The coefficient of x3x^3x3 collects −(r1+r2+r3)-(r_1 + r_2 + r_3)−(r1​+r2​+r3​) from the first product and −r4-r_4−r4​ from the second:

    −(r1+r2+r3)−r4=−(r1+r2+r3+r4)-(r_1 + r_2 + r_3) - r_4 = -(r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4)−(r1​+r2​+r3​)−r4​=−(r1​+r2​+r3​+r4​)

    So it is the sum of all four roots, negated.

    The coefficient of x2x^2x2 collects the cubic's pair sum, and r4r_4r4​ times the cubic's root sum:

    (r1r2+r1r3+r2r3)+r4(r1+r2+r3)(r_1r_2 + r_1r_3 + r_2r_3) + r_4(r_1 + r_2 + r_3)(r1​r2​+r1​r3​+r2​r3​)+r4​(r1​+r2​+r3​)

    Multiplying the second bracket out turns it into r1r4+r2r4+r3r4r_1r_4 + r_2r_4 + r_3r_4r1​r4​+r2​r4​+r3​r4​, so the coefficient has six terms in all. Those six are exactly the ways to choose two of the four roots: three pairs that avoid r4r_4r4​, which the cubic already had, and three that use it. Nothing is repeated and nothing is left out.

    The coefficient of xxx collects −r1r2r3-r_1r_2r_3−r1​r2​r3​ and −r4-r_4−r4​ times the cubic's pair sum:

    −r1r2r3−(r1r2r4+r1r3r4+r2r3r4)-r_1r_2r_3 - (r_1r_2r_4 + r_1r_3r_4 + r_2r_3r_4)−r1​r2​r3​−(r1​r2​r4​+r1​r3​r4​+r2​r3​r4​)

    Worth pausing here: the two contributions did not cancel, they combined, and both arrived negative. A term that uses three roots drags three minus signs out of three factors, and three minus signs multiply to a minus.

    The constant term is the product of the four chosen roots, (−r1)(−r2)(−r3)(−r4)=r1r2r3r4(-r_1)(-r_2)(-r_3)(-r_4) = r_1r_2r_3r_4(−r1​)(−r2​)(−r3​)(−r4​)=r1​r2​r3​r4​, positive because four minus signs cancel in pairs.

    Writing the four coefficients with the names the lesson gives them:

    (x−r1)(x−r2)(x−r3)(x−r4)=x4−e1x3+e2x2−e3x+e4(x - r_1)(x - r_2)(x - r_3)(x - r_4) = x^4 - e_1x^3 + e_2x^2 - e_3x + e_4(x−r1​)(x−r2​)(x−r3​)(x−r4​)=x4−e1​x3+e2​x2−e3​x+e4​

    Nothing was used but the distributive law, and the alternating sign is not a convention anyone chose. It counts how many roots each coefficient collects.

    Part B

    The factor theorem turns each of the four roots into a factor, and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says there are exactly four of them to turn, so ppp splits completely:

    p(x)=a4(x−r1)(x−r2)(x−r3)(x−r4)p(x) = a_4(x - r_1)(x - r_2)(x - r_3)(x - r_4)p(x)=a4​(x−r1​)(x−r2​)(x−r3​)(x−r4​)

    The identity from part A describes a product of four bare factors, whose leading coefficient is 111. This ppp has leading coefficient a4a_4a4​, so the two are not yet comparable. Divide by a4a_4a4​, which is legal because a4≠0a_4 \ne 0a4​=0, and both sides become monic:

    x4+a3a4x3+a2a4x2+a1a4x+a0a4=x4−e1x3+e2x2−e3x+e4x^4 + \frac{a_3}{a_4}x^3 + \frac{a_2}{a_4}x^2 + \frac{a_1}{a_4}x + \frac{a_0}{a_4} = x^4 - e_1x^3 + e_2x^2 - e_3x + e_4x4+a4​a3​​x3+a4​a2​​x2+a4​a1​​x+a4​a0​​=x4−e1​x3+e2​x2−e3​x+e4​

    Equal polynomials have equal coefficients, so read the four positions off in turn:

    e1=−a3a4,e2=a2a4,e3=−a1a4,e4=a0a4e_1 = -\frac{a_3}{a_4}, \qquad e_2 = \frac{a_2}{a_4}, \qquad e_3 = -\frac{a_1}{a_4}, \qquad e_4 = \frac{a_0}{a_4}e1​=−a4​a3​​,e2​=a4​a2​​,e3​=−a4​a1​​,e4​=a4​a0​​

    The division is the step that introduces a4a_4a4​, and it is the step most often dropped, because for a monic polynomial it does nothing visible. Skip it and you are comparing ppp with a monic product, which reports a4eka_4e_ka4​ek​ where eke_kek​ was wanted: every one of the four values comes out multiplied by the leading coefficient. On a quartic with leading coefficient 555 that is an answer five times the true one, with nothing in its appearance to give it away.

    Part C

    First see why the real numbers are no help. For any real xxx we have x2+4≥4x^2 + 4 \ge 4x2+4≥4, and x2−4x+13=(x−2)2+9≥9x^2 - 4x + 13 = (x - 2)^2 + 9 \ge 9x2−4x+13=(x−2)2+9≥9, so the product of the two is at least 363636 and never zero. The quartic has no real root at all.

    That matters because the formulas are not statements about whichever roots happen to be convenient. They are statements about a list of four numbers whose product of linear factors rebuilds the polynomial. Over the real numbers there is no such list here: it would be empty, and an empty list adds to 000, while the coefficients insist that e1=−−41=4e_1 = -\frac{-4}{1} = 4e1​=−1−4​=4. The formula is not wrong. It was being handed the wrong list.

    The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra supplies the right one, over the complex numbers. Solve each factor:

    x2+4=0  ⟹  x=±2ix^2 + 4 = 0 \implies x = \pm 2ix2+4=0⟹x=±2i

    x2−4x+13=0  ⟹  x=4±16−522=4±6i2=2±3ix^2 - 4x + 13 = 0 \implies x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 52}}{2} = \frac{4 \pm 6i}{2} = 2 \pm 3ix2−4x+13=0⟹x=24±16−52​​=24±6i​=2±3i

    So the list is 2i2i2i, −2i-2i−2i, 2+3i2 + 3i2+3i, 2−3i2 - 3i2−3i: four entries, arriving as two conjugate pairs, which is what real coefficients force.

    Check the first formula. The imaginary parts cancel in pairs:

    2i+(−2i)+(2+3i)+(2−3i)=4=−a3a42i + (-2i) + (2 + 3i) + (2 - 3i) = 4 = -\frac{a_3}{a_4}2i+(−2i)+(2+3i)+(2−3i)=4=−a4​a3​​

    Check the last. Each conjugate pair has a real product, (2i)(−2i)=4(2i)(-2i) = 4(2i)(−2i)=4 and (2+3i)(2−3i)=4+9=13(2 + 3i)(2 - 3i) = 4 + 9 = 13(2+3i)(2−3i)=4+9=13:

    (2i)(−2i)(2+3i)(2−3i)=4×13=52=a0a4(2i)(-2i)(2 + 3i)(2 - 3i) = 4 \times 13 = 52 = \frac{a_0}{a_4}(2i)(−2i)(2+3i)(2−3i)=4×13=52=a4​a0​​

    Both agree. The coefficients are real, every root is not, and the formulas never noticed, because what they were promised was a complete list and a complete list is what they were given.

    In one line

    Multiplying the cubic expansion by (x−r4)(x - r_4)(x−r4​) and collecting gives x4−e1x3+e2x2−e3x+e4x^4 - e_1x^3 + e_2x^2 - e_3x + e_4x4−e1​x3+e2​x2−e3​x+e4​ once the coefficients are named, and written out the x2x^2x2 coefficient is r1r2+r1r3+r1r4+r2r3+r2r4+r3r4r_1r_2 + r_1r_3 + r_1r_4 + r_2r_3 + r_2r_4 + r_3r_4r1​r2​+r1​r3​+r1​r4​+r2​r3​+r2​r4​+r3​r4​: the three pairs the cubic already had, plus the three that pair r4r_4r4​ with an earlier root. Matching that against a4x4+a3x3+a2x2+a1x+a0a_4x^4 + a_3x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_1x + a_0a4​x4+a3​x3+a2​x2+a1​x+a0​ once both sides are monic gives e1=−a3a4e_1 = -\frac{a_3}{a_4}e1​=−a4​a3​​, e2=a2a4e_2 = \frac{a_2}{a_4}e2​=a4​a2​​, e3=−a1a4e_3 = -\frac{a_1}{a_4}e3​=−a4​a1​​ and e4=a0a4e_4 = \frac{a_0}{a_4}e4​=a4​a0​​; skip the division and every value comes out a4a_4a4​ times the true one. For x4−4x3+17x2−16x+52x^4 - 4x^3 + 17x^2 - 16x + 52x4−4x3+17x2−16x+52 no real number is a root, so the list the formulas describe is the complex one, 2i2i2i, −2i-2i−2i, 2+3i2 + 3i2+3i, 2−3i2 - 3i2−3i, which delivers e1=4e_1 = 4e1​=4 and e4=52e_4 = 52e4​=52 exactly as the coefficients require.

    Try a similar problem (Optional)

    Same idea, different numbers. Work it on paper, then check yourself the same way.

    Multiply the degree-four identity by (x−r5)(x - r_5)(x−r5​) and read off the coefficient of x3x^3x3 and the constant term for five roots. Give the sign each one carries, and say what decides it.

    The answer

    The expansion is x5−e1x4+e2x3−e3x2+e4x−e5x^5 - e_1x^4 + e_2x^3 - e_3x^2 + e_4x - e_5x5−e1​x4+e2​x3−e3​x2+e4​x−e5​. The coefficient of x3x^3x3 is +e2+e_2+e2​, the ten products of two roots, positive because two minus signs cancel; the constant term is −e5-e_5−e5​, the product of all five, negative because five minus signs do not.

    Multiplying x4−e1x3+e2x2−e3x+e4x^4 - e_1x^3 + e_2x^2 - e_3x + e_4x4−e1​x3+e2​x2−e3​x+e4​ by (x−r5)(x - r_5)(x−r5​) and collecting powers gives

    x5−e1x4+e2x3−e3x2+e4x−e5x^5 - e_1x^4 + e_2x^3 - e_3x^2 + e_4x - e_5x5−e1​x4+e2​x3−e3​x2+e4​x−e5​

    where every eke_kek​ now runs over all five roots. Take the two positions asked for.

    The coefficient of x3x^3x3 is +e2+e_2+e2​, and it collects every product of two of the five roots: the six pairs among the first four, which the quartic already carried, plus the four that pair r5r_5r5​ with each of them, so ten terms. Its sign is plus because a term that uses two roots drags two minus signs, and two minus signs cancel.

    The constant term is −e5-e_5−e5​, the product of all five roots, negated. Five roots means five minus signs, and five is odd.

    Notice what decides each sign. It is not the degree of the polynomial and not whether the quantity is called a sum or a product. It is kkk, the number of roots the term collects, and the sign is (−1)k(-1)^k(−1)k.

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    e1=0e_1 = 0e1​=0, e2=−32e_2 = -\frac{3}{2}e2​=−23​, e3=−34e_3 = -\frac{3}{4}e3​=−43​, e4=12e_4 = \frac{1}{2}e4​=21​. The absent term is the coefficient a3=0a_3 = 0a3​=0, and it forces the four roots to add to exactly 000.

    Part C

    It reports no repeat: both readings give 000, though every root there is repeated. A sound test counts, setting the nnn entries the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra puts on the list against the number of distinct values. Totals cannot: extra copies can add to nothing. One half survives, since a disagreement does prove a repeat.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Write the coefficients out first, including the position that has no term. An absent power is not a gap in the polynomial; it is a coefficient equal to zero:

    a4=4,a3=0,a2=−6,a1=3,a0=2a_4 = 4, \quad a_3 = 0, \quad a_2 = -6, \quad a_1 = 3, \quad a_0 = 2a4​=4,a3​=0,a2​=−6,a1​=3,a0​=2

    Now apply ek=(−1)ka4−ka4e_k = (-1)^k\frac{a_{4-k}}{a_4}ek​=(−1)ka4​a4−k​​ four times, dividing by 444 every time and reading the parity of kkk every time:

    e1=−04=0,e2=−64=−32e_1 = -\frac{0}{4} = 0, \qquad e_2 = \frac{-6}{4} = -\frac{3}{2}e1​=−40​=0,e2​=4−6​=−23​

    e3=−34,e4=24=12e_3 = -\frac{3}{4}, \qquad e_4 = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}e3​=−43​,e4​=42​=21​

    The absent x3x^3x3 term did not excuse you from the first formula. It supplied the numerator, and the numerator was 000.

    That is worth reading back into the roots, because it is a constraint and not an absence. e1e_1e1​ is the sum of all four roots, so this quartic's four roots add to exactly 000. Whatever they are, and none of them is obvious from the coefficients, they balance. Compare that with e2=−32e_2 = -\frac{3}{2}e2​=−23​, which is a genuine number rather than a coincidence of missing ink: both were read the same way, from the coefficient sitting kkk places down from the leading one and a division by that leading 444.

    Part B

    The factorization 2(x+1)2(x−3)2(x + 1)^2(x - 3)2(x+1)2(x−3) names the root −1-1−1 with multiplicity two and the root 333 with multiplicity one, so the complete list has three entries:

    −1,−1,3-1, \quad -1, \quad 3−1,−1,3

    From that list, treating the two copies of −1-1−1 as two separate roots that happen to be equal:

    e1=−1+(−1)+3=1e_1 = -1 + (-1) + 3 = 1e1​=−1+(−1)+3=1

    e2=(−1)(−1)+(−1)(3)+(−1)(3)=1−3−3=−5e_2 = (-1)(-1) + (-1)(3) + (-1)(3) = 1 - 3 - 3 = -5e2​=(−1)(−1)+(−1)(3)+(−1)(3)=1−3−3=−5

    e3=(−1)(−1)(3)=3e_3 = (-1)(-1)(3) = 3e3​=(−1)(−1)(3)=3

    From the coefficients, with a3=2a_3 = 2a3​=2, a2=−2a_2 = -2a2​=−2, a1=−10a_1 = -10a1​=−10 and a0=−6a_0 = -6a0​=−6:

    e1=−−22=1,e2=−102=−5,e3=−−62=3e_1 = -\frac{-2}{2} = 1, \qquad e_2 = \frac{-10}{2} = -5, \qquad e_3 = -\frac{-6}{2} = 3e1​=−2−2​=1,e2​=2−10​=−5,e3​=−2−6​=3

    The two routes agree in all three places, and note that they had to agree by different-looking arithmetic: one route multiplied roots, the other divided coefficients by 222.

    Now shorten the list to one entry per distinct value, −1-1−1 and 333, and run the first route again. The sum becomes −1+3=2-1 + 3 = 2−1+3=2. There is now only one pair, so the pair sum becomes (−1)(3)=−3(-1)(3) = -3(−1)(3)=−3. And the product of everything on the list becomes (−1)(3)=−3(-1)(3) = -3(−1)(3)=−3.

    So the shortened list reports 222, −3-3−3, −3-3−3 where the truth is 111, −5-5−5, 333. Every one of the three is wrong, and the third has even changed sign. The place where the damage is easiest to see is e2e_2e2​: the full list contributes the term (−1)(−1)(-1)(-1)(−1)(−1), the product of the two copies of the repeated root, and that term simply has nowhere to come from once one copy has been thrown away. Multiplicity is not a bookkeeping nicety here. It is the difference between a true statement and a false one.

    Part C

    Run the test as it stands. The polynomial is (x2−9)2(x^2 - 9)^2(x2−9)2, so its root list is 333, 333, −3-3−3, −3-3−3, and the coefficients give

    e1=−01=0e_1 = -\frac{0}{1} = 0e1​=−10​=0

    since there is no x3x^3x3 term. The distinct values are 333 and −3-3−3, and they add to 000 as well. The two readings agree, so the test returns a verdict of no repeated root, and it is wrong four times over: every entry on that list is one of a repeated pair.

    Now ask why it failed, because the failure is not bad luck. e1e_1e1​ is a single number, and it is being asked to report on a list of four entries. The two extra copies changed the total by 3+(−3)=03 + (-3) = 03+(−3)=0, so the very arithmetic meant to detect them destroyed the evidence. Any test built on a symmetric total can be defeated the same way: arrange the repeats so that what they contribute to that particular total is nothing. A total compresses a list into one number, and a repeat is a fact about the list that the compression is free to discard.

    What a test for a repeated root has to compare is counts, not totals. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra fixes the length of the complete list at nnn, the degree, and a repeated root is exactly the situation where fewer than nnn distinct values are spread over those nnn places. So the honest comparison is nnn against the number of distinct values, and both sides of it are counts, neither of which any symmetric sum reports.

    One half of the classmate's test does survive, and it is worth keeping. If the two readings disagree there must be a repeat, because with no repeats the root list holds each value exactly once, so the two readings are sums of the very same collection and cannot differ. A disagreement is therefore real evidence. An agreement is no evidence at all, and the better habit is not to depend on either: the shortened list is not an approximation of the true one, so build the complete list with multiplicity from the start and there is nothing left to detect.

    In one line

    For 4x4−6x2+3x+24x^4 - 6x^2 + 3x + 24x4−6x2+3x+2 the absent x3x^3x3 term is a3=0a_3 = 0a3​=0, giving e1=0e_1 = 0e1​=0, and then e2=−32e_2 = -\frac{3}{2}e2​=−23​, e3=−34e_3 = -\frac{3}{4}e3​=−43​, e4=12e_4 = \frac{1}{2}e4​=21​; the value e1=0e_1 = 0e1​=0 says the four roots add to nothing. For 2x3−2x2−10x−6=2(x+1)2(x−3)2x^3 - 2x^2 - 10x - 6 = 2(x + 1)^2(x - 3)2x3−2x2−10x−6=2(x+1)2(x−3) the list is −1,−1,3-1, -1, 3−1,−1,3, and both routes give e1=1e_1 = 1e1​=1, e2=−5e_2 = -5e2​=−5, e3=3e_3 = 3e3​=3, where one entry per distinct value would have given 222, −3-3−3, −3-3−3, wrong in all three places. On x4−18x2+81=(x2−9)2x^4 - 18x^2 + 81 = (x^2 - 9)^2x4−18x2+81=(x2−9)2, every root of which is repeated, the classmate's test returns no repeat, because both readings give 000: a total can always be defeated that way, so a sound test compares the nnn entries of the complete list against the number of distinct values, and only the disagreement half of the test is safe.

  3. 3

    3. Three lengths from three totals . Application, 14 points. Question 3 of 5.

    Application 14 pts

    A specimen case is a rectangular box built from metal edging along all twelve of its edges and glass panels covering all six of its faces. An order sheet for one never gives the three side lengths. It gives what the framer has to buy and what the case has to hold: the total length of edging, the total area of glass, and the capacity inside. Two order sheets are below, both measured in centimetres.

    1. A
      Part A.

      The first sheet calls for 525252 cm of edging, 108108108 square centimetres of glass, and a capacity of 727272 cubic centimetres. Writing the three side lengths as xxx, yyy and zzz, turn each of those three figures into an equation in those lengths. Then assemble from them a single monic cubic whose roots are the three side lengths.

      Model the situation Name your unknown first, then write every other quantity in terms of that one letter. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Find the three side lengths of the first case, and check them against all three figures on the order sheet, not only against the one that led you to them.

      Carry your own answer forward Work from the cubic you assembled in part A. If yours differs, carry your own version forward: what is marked here is the search for its roots and the check against all three figures.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      A second sheet calls for 282828 cm of edging, 222222 square centimetres of glass, and a capacity of 444 cubic centimetres. The framer marks their cuts against a scale, so any side length they can actually set out is a rational number of centimetres. Decide whether a case can be built to this sheet on that scale, and be exact about what your argument settles and what it leaves open.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 6 points

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 3

      Nothing on an order sheet is a side length, but every figure on it is a total that stays put when two of the sides are swapped. That is the kind of quantity this lesson reads off a polynomial.

    2. Hint 2 of 3 · Part B

      The cubic is monic with whole-number coefficients, so a rational root has to be a whole number dividing the constant term. Once one is found, what is left is short enough to finish outright.

    3. Hint 3 of 3 · Part C

      Build the second cubic exactly as you built the first. Then ask which numbers a complete candidate list is capable of ruling out, and which numbers it was never in a position to say anything about.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    The three figures give 4(x+y+z)=524(x + y + z) = 524(x+y+z)=52, 2(xy+xz+yz)=1082(xy + xz + yz) = 1082(xy+xz+yz)=108 and xyz=72xyz = 72xyz=72, so e1=13e_1 = 13e1​=13, e2=54e_2 = 54e2​=54 and e3=72e_3 = 72e3​=72, and the cubic is t3−13t2+54t−72t^3 - 13t^2 + 54t - 72t3−13t2+54t−72.

    Part B

    The side lengths are 333 cm, 444 cm and 666 cm. They account for all three figures: 525252 cm of edging, 108108108 square centimetres of glass, and a capacity of 727272 cubic centimetres.

    • The same three lengths given in any order describe the same case
    • 666 cm by 444 cm by 333 cm is the same case read the other way round

    Part C

    Not on that scale. The cubic is t3−7t2+11t−4t^3 - 7t^2 + 11t - 4t3−7t2+11t−4, and not one of its six rational candidates ±1\pm 1±1, ±2\pm 2±2, ±4\pm 4±4 is a root, so no side length for this sheet is rational. What that leaves open is whether the three figures can be met at all, since a candidate list speaks only about fractions.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Turn each figure into an equation. A rectangular box has twelve edges, four of each length, so the edging is

    4(x+y+z)=524(x + y + z) = 524(x+y+z)=52

    It has six faces in three matching pairs, so the glass is

    2(xy+xz+yz)=1082(xy + xz + yz) = 1082(xy+xz+yz)=108

    And the capacity is the product of the three lengths:

    xyz=72xyz = 72xyz=72

    Look at what the left sides are. They are the sum of the three lengths, the sum of their three pairwise products, and their product: precisely e1e_1e1​, e2e_2e2​ and e3e_3e3​ for the list x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z. That is why the order sheet can be read at all. Every figure on it is symmetric, unchanged if two sides are swapped, which is exactly the kind of quantity these formulas handle.

    Divide the first equation by 444 and the second by 222:

    e1=13,e2=54,e3=72e_1 = 13, \qquad e_2 = 54, \qquad e_3 = 72e1​=13,e2​=54,e3​=72

    Now run the formulas backwards. A monic cubic with roots xxx, yyy, zzz is t3−e1t2+e2t−e3t^3 - e_1t^2 + e_2t - e_3t3−e1​t2+e2​t−e3​, with the signs alternating, so

    t3−13t2+54t−72t^3 - 13t^2 + 54t - 72t3−13t2+54t−72

    The three side lengths are the roots of that cubic. Nothing has been solved yet; what has happened is that three equations in three unknowns, two of them not linear, have become one polynomial in one unknown.

    Part B

    The cubic t3−13t2+54t−72t^3 - 13t^2 + 54t - 72t3−13t2+54t−72 is monic with whole-number coefficients, so any rational root is a whole number dividing 727272. Start at the small divisors, since a side length of a case this size is unlikely to be large:

    1−13+54−72=−30,8−52+108−72=−81 - 13 + 54 - 72 = -30, \qquad 8 - 52 + 108 - 72 = -81−13+54−72=−30,8−52+108−72=−8

    Neither 111 nor 222 is a root. Try 333:

    27−117+162−72=027 - 117 + 162 - 72 = 027−117+162−72=0

    So 333 is a root, and the hunt is nearly over: dividing it out leaves a quadratic, which can be finished outright. Synthetic division by 333 on the coefficients 1,−13,54,−721, -13, 54, -721,−13,54,−72 brings down the 111, then −13+3=−10-13 + 3 = -10−13+3=−10, then 54−30=2454 - 30 = 2454−30=24, then −72+72=0-72 + 72 = 0−72+72=0:

    t3−13t2+54t−72=(t−3)(t2−10t+24)t^3 - 13t^2 + 54t - 72 = (t - 3)(t^2 - 10t + 24)t3−13t2+54t−72=(t−3)(t2−10t+24)

    The remainder of 000 confirms the root, and the quadratic factors as (t−4)(t−6)(t - 4)(t - 6)(t−4)(t−6), as multiplying it back out confirms. So the three roots are 333, 444 and 666, and those are the three side lengths in centimetres.

    Check them against the whole order sheet rather than one line of it. Edging: 4(3+4+6)=4×13=524(3 + 4 + 6) = 4 \times 13 = 524(3+4+6)=4×13=52 cm. Glass: 2(12+18+24)=2×54=1082(12 + 18 + 24) = 2 \times 54 = 1082(12+18+24)=2×54=108 square centimetres. Capacity:

    3×4×6=72 cubic centimetres3 \times 4 \times 6 = 72 \text{ cubic centimetres}3×4×6=72 cubic centimetres

    All three figures are accounted for, which is the check worth running: the cubic was built from all three, so an error in any one of them would have shown up here.

    Part C

    Set the second sheet up exactly as the first. Dividing the edging by 444 and the glass by 222:

    e1=7,e2=11,e3=4e_1 = 7, \qquad e_2 = 11, \qquad e_3 = 4e1​=7,e2​=11,e3​=4

    so the cubic whose roots are the three side lengths is

    t3−7t2+11t−4t^3 - 7t^2 + 11t - 4t3−7t2+11t−4

    It is monic with whole-number coefficients, so a rational root has to be a whole number dividing 444, and the entire candidate list is ±1\pm 1±1, ±2\pm 2±2 and ±4\pm 4±4. The three negative entries are already ruled out by the situation, since a side length is positive, but test all six so that the verdict rests on the complete list:

    1−7+11−4=1,8−28+22−4=−21 - 7 + 11 - 4 = 1, \qquad 8 - 28 + 22 - 4 = -21−7+11−4=1,8−28+22−4=−2

    64−112+44−4=−864 - 112 + 44 - 4 = -864−112+44−4=−8

    and the three negative candidates give −23-23−23, −62-62−62 and −224-224−224. Not one of the six is zero, and every rational root of the cubic would have had to appear among them. So the cubic has no rational root at all, and therefore no side length meeting this sheet is a rational number of centimetres. Nothing the framer can set out on that scale will fit, and the failure is exact rather than a matter of tolerance: it is not that the numbers come out awkward, it is that no fraction whatever is a solution.

    Compare that with the first sheet, where the same sweep found a root at the third candidate it tried. The two sheets were read the same way and the machinery behaved identically. All that differs is what the candidate list happened to contain.

    Now be exact about the size of the conclusion, because this is where a sweep is most often overread. A candidate list is a statement about fractions and about nothing else. It says no rational number is a side length here. It does not say the three figures are impossible, and it does not locate, approximate or describe any length that might meet them. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra still puts three roots on the list, and Vieta's formulas still describe them: what those roots are, and whether they are real, is a question this argument never asked and cannot answer.

    In one line

    The first sheet gives 4(x+y+z)=524(x + y + z) = 524(x+y+z)=52, 2(xy+xz+yz)=1082(xy + xz + yz) = 1082(xy+xz+yz)=108 and xyz=72xyz = 72xyz=72, so e1=13e_1 = 13e1​=13, e2=54e_2 = 54e2​=54, e3=72e_3 = 72e3​=72 and the side lengths are the roots of t3−13t2+54t−72=(t−3)(t−4)(t−6)t^3 - 13t^2 + 54t - 72 = (t - 3)(t - 4)(t - 6)t3−13t2+54t−72=(t−3)(t−4)(t−6): a case 333 cm by 444 cm by 666 cm, which accounts for all three figures. The second sheet gives e1=7e_1 = 7e1​=7, e2=11e_2 = 11e2​=11, e3=4e_3 = 4e3​=4 and the cubic t3−7t2+11t−4t^3 - 7t^2 + 11t - 4t3−7t2+11t−4, whose rational candidates ±1\pm 1±1, ±2\pm 2±2, ±4\pm 4±4 return 111, −23-23−23, −2-2−2, −62-62−62, −8-8−8 and −224-224−224. No side length for that sheet is a rational number, so the framer cannot set one out. That is the whole of what the sweep settles: whether the three figures can be met at all by any lengths is a question a list of fractions was never able to reach.

    Try a similar problem (Optional)

    Same idea, different numbers. Work it on paper, then check yourself the same way.

    A third sheet calls for 323232 cm of edging, 505050 square centimetres of glass, and a capacity of 262626 cubic centimetres. Decide whether a case can be built to it.

    The answer

    No case can be built. The figures give e1=8e_1 = 8e1​=8, e2=25e_2 = 25e2​=25, e3=26e_3 = 26e3​=26 and the cubic t3−8t2+25t−26=(t−2)(t2−6t+13)t^3 - 8t^2 + 25t - 26 = (t - 2)(t^2 - 6t + 13)t3−8t2+25t−26=(t−2)(t2−6t+13), whose roots are 222, 3+2i3 + 2i3+2i and 3−2i3 - 2i3−2i: only one of the three is a real number, and three side lengths would have to be three real positive numbers.

    Divide the edging by 444 and the glass by 222 to get the three symmetric sums of the side lengths:

    e1=8,e2=25,e3=26e_1 = 8, \qquad e_2 = 25, \qquad e_3 = 26e1​=8,e2​=25,e3​=26

    so the side lengths are the roots of

    t3−8t2+25t−26t^3 - 8t^2 + 25t - 26t3−8t2+25t−26

    Any rational root is a whole number dividing 262626, leaving 111, 222, 131313 and 262626 with either sign. At t=1t = 1t=1 the value is 1−8+25−26=−81 - 8 + 25 - 26 = -81−8+25−26=−8, and at t=2t = 2t=2:

    8−32+50−26=08 - 32 + 50 - 26 = 08−32+50−26=0

    Divide that root out. Synthetic division by 222 on 1,−8,25,−261, -8, 25, -261,−8,25,−26 gives 111, then −6-6−6, then 131313, remainder 000, so

    t3−8t2+25t−26=(t−2)(t2−6t+13)t^3 - 8t^2 + 25t - 26 = (t - 2)(t^2 - 6t + 13)t3−8t2+25t−26=(t−2)(t2−6t+13)

    The quadratic has discriminant 36−52=−1636 - 52 = -1636−52=−16, so its roots are not real:

    t=6±−162=6±4i2=3±2it = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{-16}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm 4i}{2} = 3 \pm 2it=26±−16​​=26±4i​=3±2i

    The complete root list is 222, 3+2i3 + 2i3+2i, 3−2i3 - 2i3−2i, the two non-real entries arriving as a conjugate pair exactly as real coefficients force. If a case existed to this sheet, its three side lengths would be three real positive numbers with those symmetric sums, so they would be three real roots of this cubic. It has one. So no case can be built, and this time the verdict is settled outright rather than left open: what failed is not the formulas, which delivered a complete list of three, but the demand that all three entries be real lengths.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Each factorization hands over its roots, so the true product needs no formula at all, which is what makes these two cases a fair test of one.

    The cubic has roots 111, −2-2−2 and 555, so their product is

    1×(−2)×5=−101 \times (-2) \times 5 = -101×(−2)×5=−10

    The rule predicts a0an=202=10\frac{a_0}{a_n} = \frac{20}{2} = 10an​a0​​=220​=10. Right size, wrong sign. The rule fails here.

    The quartic has roots 111, −1-1−1, 222 and −3-3−3, so their product is

    1×(−1)×2×(−3)=61 \times (-1) \times 2 \times (-3) = 61×(−1)×2×(−3)=6

    The rule predicts a0an=122=6\frac{a_0}{a_n} = \frac{12}{2} = 6an​a0​​=212​=6. It succeeds here.

    So the rule is not simply wrong, which is what makes it durable: one of these two tests would have confirmed it. Now notice how little separates the two polynomials. Both have leading coefficient 222, so that cannot be what decides the verdict, and dividing by it was done the same way in both. The one thing that differs is the number of roots. The product of all the roots is the symmetric sum that collects every one of them, so it drags nnn minus signs out of the nnn factors, and nnn minus signs multiply to (−1)n(-1)^n(−1)n: minus for the cubic, plus for the quartic. The corrected rule carries that factor:

    r1r2⋯rn=(−1)na0anr_1r_2\cdots r_n = (-1)^n\frac{a_0}{a_n}r1​r2​⋯rn​=(−1)nan​a0​​

    Check it on both. For the cubic, (−1)3202=−10(-1)^3\frac{20}{2} = -10(−1)3220​=−10, matching. For the quartic, (−1)4122=6(-1)^4\frac{12}{2} = 6(−1)4212​=6, matching too.

    Part B

    Choose the value of xxx that kills everything but the constant term. In standard form every term except the last carries a factor of xxx, so

    p(0)=a0p(0) = a_0p(0)=a0​

    Evaluate the factored form at the same place. Each factor (x−ri)(x - r_i)(x−ri​) becomes −ri-r_i−ri​:

    p(0)=an(−r1)(−r2)⋯(−rn)p(0) = a_n(-r_1)(-r_2)\cdots(-r_n)p(0)=an​(−r1​)(−r2​)⋯(−rn​)

    There are nnn factors and each contributes one minus sign, so pull all nnn of them out at once:

    p(0)=(−1)nanr1r2⋯rnp(0) = (-1)^na_nr_1r_2\cdots r_np(0)=(−1)nan​r1​r2​⋯rn​

    The two evaluations are of the same polynomial at the same point, so they are equal:

    a0=(−1)nanr1r2⋯rna_0 = (-1)^na_nr_1r_2\cdots r_na0​=(−1)nan​r1​r2​⋯rn​

    Multiply both sides by (−1)n(-1)^n(−1)n, which is legal because (−1)n(−1)n=1(-1)^n(-1)^n = 1(−1)n(−1)n=1, and divide by ana_nan​, which is legal because an≠0a_n \ne 0an​=0:

    r1r2⋯rn=(−1)na0anr_1r_2\cdots r_n = (-1)^n\frac{a_0}{a_n}r1​r2​⋯rn​=(−1)nan​a0​​

    That is the corrected rule, for every degree at once, and the whole proof was one substitution.

    Now the diagnosis. The sign is not decided by the degree as such; it is decided by how many roots the term collects, and the constant term happens to collect all of them, which is why the degree ends up controlling it here. A quadratic has two roots, two minus signs come out, and two minus signs cancel. So on quadratics the original rule and the corrected rule give the same answer every single time, and a student could test it on a hundred of them without ever seeing a discrepancy. The rule is not half remembered. It is a true statement about even degrees that was quietly promoted to a statement about all of them.

    Part C

    An "exactly when" is two claims, and here they have very different fates.

    Forwards, if nnn is even then (−1)n=1(-1)^n = 1(−1)n=1, so part B reads r1r2⋯rn=a0anr_1r_2\cdots r_n = \frac{a_0}{a_n}r1​r2​⋯rn​=an​a0​​ directly. That half is sound.

    Backwards, the claim is that equality forces the degree to be even, and one polynomial breaks it. Take

    x3+2x2−8x=x(x+4)(x−2)x^3 + 2x^2 - 8x = x(x + 4)(x - 2)x3+2x2−8x=x(x+4)(x−2)

    Its roots are 000, −4-4−4 and 222, so their product is 000. Its constant term is 000 and its leading coefficient is 111, so a0an=0\frac{a_0}{a_n} = 0an​a0​​=0 as well. The two sides agree, and the degree is 333, which is odd. The reverse direction is false.

    What happened is that both sides were nothing at all, so the sign in front of one of them had nothing to act on. Chasing that down settles the general case too. At odd degree part B gives r1r2⋯rn=−a0anr_1r_2\cdots r_n = -\frac{a_0}{a_n}r1​r2​⋯rn​=−an​a0​​, and this can equal a0an\frac{a_0}{a_n}an​a0​​ only when

    a0an=−a0an,that is, whena0=0\frac{a_0}{a_n} = -\frac{a_0}{a_n}, \quad \text{that is, when} \quad a_0 = 0an​a0​​=−an​a0​​,that is, whena0​=0

    So the only odd-degree escapes are the polynomials with constant term 000, which are exactly the polynomials having 000 as a root, since p(0)=a0p(0) = a_0p(0)=a0​.

    Add the condition a0≠0a_0 \ne 0a0​=0 and the repaired claim holds both ways. Forwards is unchanged. Backwards, equality plus a0≠0a_0 \ne 0a0​=0 forces (−1)n=1(-1)^n = 1(−1)n=1, so nnn is even. Both directions, tested separately, which is the only way an "exactly when" can honestly be checked.

    There is a second repair, and it is worth having because it throws nothing away. Rather than excluding the awkward case, absorb it: equality holds exactly when nnn is even OR a0=0a_0 = 0a0​=0. Both halves of that are already proved above. Forwards, an even degree gives equality by part B, and a0=0a_0 = 0a0​=0 gives it by making both sides 000 whatever the degree. Backwards, equality means a0an((−1)n−1)=0\frac{a_0}{a_n}\bigl((-1)^n - 1\bigr) = 0an​a0​​((−1)n−1)=0, so one of the two factors vanishes, which is exactly the two cases named. Either repair is correct; the first narrows the claim and the second widens it.

    In one line

    The rule fails on 2x3−8x2−14x+202x^3 - 8x^2 - 14x + 202x3−8x2−14x+20, where it predicts 101010 against a true product of −10-10−10, and passes on 2x4+2x3−14x2−2x+122x^4 + 2x^3 - 14x^2 - 2x + 122x4+2x3−14x2−2x+12, where both come to 666. The two share a leading coefficient of 222, so degree is the only thing separating the verdicts. Evaluating p(x)=an(x−r1)⋯(x−rn)p(x) = a_n(x - r_1)\cdots(x - r_n)p(x)=an​(x−r1​)⋯(x−rn​) and its standard form at x=0x = 0x=0 gives a0=(−1)nanr1r2⋯rna_0 = (-1)^na_nr_1r_2\cdots r_na0​=(−1)nan​r1​r2​⋯rn​, so the roots multiply to (−1)na0an(-1)^n\frac{a_0}{a_n}(−1)nan​a0​​; a quadratic has n=2n = 2n=2 and (−1)2=1(-1)^2 = 1(−1)2=1, which is why quadratics can never expose the error. The repair "equality exactly when the degree is even" holds forwards but not backwards: x3+2x2−8xx^3 + 2x^2 - 8xx3+2x2−8x has roots 000, −4-4−4, 222 and both sides equal 000 at odd degree. Requiring a0≠0a_0 \ne 0a0​=0 makes it true in both directions, and so does widening it to "nnn even or a0=0a_0 = 0a0​=0".

    Decide whether the rule "the roots of a polynomial add up to an−1an\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}an​an−1​​" is ever correct, and if so for exactly which polynomials.

    The answer

    It is correct exactly when an−1=0a_{n-1} = 0an−1​=0, where both sides come to 000, and for no other polynomial of any degree, because the sum of the roots always collects one root per term and so always carries one minus sign.

    Vieta gives the sum of the roots as

The reason is worth stating, because it is the opposite of the situation with the product: a term in the sum of the roots collects exactly one root, so it drags exactly one minus sign, and one is odd at every degree. The parity here is fixed by k=1k = 1k=1, not by nnn.

    So the proposed rule agrees with the truth only when

    an−1an=−an−1an\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n} = -\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}an​an−1​​=−an​an−1​​

    Adding an−1an\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}an​an−1​​ to both sides gives 2an−1an=02\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n} = 02an​an−1​​=0, and since an≠0a_n \ne 0an​=0 this says an−1=0a_{n-1} = 0an−1​=0.

    So the rule is correct exactly for the polynomials whose second coefficient is zero, where both sides are 000 and the sign has nothing to act on, and it is wrong for every other polynomial of every degree. Unlike the product rule, which is right for half the degrees, this one is never rescued by the degree at all.

    Answer and solution

    The answer

    Part A

    e1=2e_1 = 2e1​=2 and e2=92e_2 = \frac{9}{2}e2​=29​. Written out, e2=r1r2+r1r3+r1r4+r2r3+r2r4+r3r4e_2 = r_1r_2 + r_1r_3 + r_1r_4 + r_2r_3 + r_2r_4 + r_3r_4e2​=r1​r2​+r1​r3​+r1​r4​+r2​r3​+r2​r4​+r3​r4​: six terms, each the product of two different entries of the root list.

    • The six products written in any order name the same sum

    Part B

    Squaring e1e_1e1​ produces the four squares plus each of the six mixed products twice, once as rirjr_ir_jri​rj​ and once as rjrir_jr_irj​ri​, so the sum of the squares is e12−2e2e_1^2 - 2e_2e12​−2e2​.     Part C

    They cannot: a real square is never negative, so with four real roots the squares would total at least 000, not −5-5−5. Real coefficients pair the non-real roots, so at least two of the four are not real. The reverse reading fails: x4+1x^4 + 1x4+1 has e1=e2=0e_1 = e_2 = 0e1​=e2​=0, so a sum of squares of 000, yet it is never below 111 for real xxx.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Read the coefficients off first: a4=2a_4 = 2a4​=2, a3=−4a_3 = -4a3​=−4, a2=9a_2 = 9a2​=9. Then apply the formula twice, dividing by the leading 222 each time and taking the sign from the parity of kkk:

    e1=−a3a4=−−42=2,e2=a2a4=92e_1 = -\frac{a_3}{a_4} = -\frac{-4}{2} = 2, \qquad e_2 = \frac{a_2}{a_4} = \frac{9}{2}e1​=−a4​a3​​=−2−4​=2,e2​=a4​a2​​=29​

    Neither division can be skipped: this quartic is not monic, and the coefficients −4-4−4 and 999 on their own would report values twice as large as the truth.

    Written out in the roots, e2e_2e2​ takes two different entries of the list at a time and adds every such product once:

    e2=r1r2+r1r3+r1r4+r2r3+r2r4+r3r4e_2 = r_1r_2 + r_1r_3 + r_1r_4 + r_2r_3 + r_2r_4 + r_3r_4e2​=r1​r2​+r1​r3​+r1​r4​+r2​r3​+r2​r4​+r3​r4​

    Six terms, because there are six ways to choose two entries from four when the order of the two does not matter. Read carefully what a term is: a product of two DIFFERENT entries. No term of e2e_2e2​ multiplies an entry by itself, so e2e_2e2​ is not the sum of the squares of the roots, however similar the two may sound.

    "Different entries" is not the same as "different values", though. Had two entries of this list happened to be equal, their product would still be one of the six terms, and it would then be a square: a repeated root contributes its own square to e2e_2e2​ through the two separate copies of itself. What never happens is one entry pairing with itself.

    Part B

    Square the sum of the four roots by multiplying it by itself the long way, taking one entry from each copy of the bracket:

    e12=(r1+r2+r3+r4)(r1+r2+r3+r4)e_1^2 = (r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4)(r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4)e12​=(r1​+r2​+r3​+r4​)(r1​+r2​+r3​+r4​)

    The choices split into two kinds. Four of them take the same entry from both copies, giving r12r_1^2r12​, r22r_2^2r22​, r32r_3^2r32​ and r42r_4^2r42​. Every other choice takes two different entries, and each such pair arises twice, once as rirjr_ir_jri​rj​ and once as rjrir_jr_irj​ri​, because the two copies of the bracket are ordered and the pair can be drawn from them either way round. So the mixed products contribute each of the six terms of e2e_2e2​ exactly twice:

    e12=(r12+r22+r32+r42)+2e2e_1^2 = (r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2 + r_4^2) + 2e_2e12​=(r12​+r22​+r32​+r42​)+2e2​

    The factor of 222 is not decoration. It is a count of the orders in which one pair can be drawn. Rearranging:

    r12+r22+r32+r42=e12−2e2r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2 + r_4^2 = e_1^2 - 2e_2r12​+r22​+r32​+r42​=e12​−2e2​

    Nothing in that argument used the fact that there were four roots, so the same identity holds at any degree.

    Now evaluate it for ppp, using the two values from part A:

    r12+r22+r32+r42=22−2×92=4−9=−5r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2 + r_4^2 = 2^2 - 2 \times \frac{9}{2} = 4 - 9 = -5r12​+r22​+r32​+r42​=22−2×29​=4−9=−5

    Set that against e2=92e_2 = \frac{9}{2}e2​=29​. The two quantities are not equal, they are not close, and one is negative while the other is positive. They are different quantities: e2e_2e2​ is a symmetric sum that Vieta hands over directly from a coefficient, and the sum of the squares is a derived quantity that has to be built out of two of them first. Note also what has just been computed. No root of ppp has been produced here, and the rational root theorem has ruled out only the kind of number it is able to rule out, and yet the sum of the squares of all four is known exactly.

    Part C

    Suppose all four roots of ppp were real. The square of a real number is never negative, so each of r12r_1^2r12​, r22r_2^2r22​, r32r_3^2r32​ and r42r_4^2r42​ would be at least 000, and a sum of four such numbers would be at least 000 too:

    r12+r22+r32+r42≥0r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2 + r_4^2 \ge 0r12​+r22​+r32​+r42​≥0

    But part B computed that sum, and it is −5-5−5. So the supposition is impossible and at least one root of ppp is not real. One more step is available for free: the coefficients of ppp are real, so its non-real roots come in conjugate pairs, and therefore at least two of the four are non-real.

    That is a striking amount to know about four numbers none of which has been produced. No root was located, approximated or even bounded here, and the argument turns on nothing more than the fact that squares of real numbers do not come out negative.

    Now the reverse reading, which has to be tested separately rather than assumed to come along. It claims that a sum of squares that is positive or zero would force all the roots to be real. Take

    x4+1x^4 + 1x4+1

    Its x3x^3x3 and x2x^2x2 coefficients are both 000, so e1=0e_1 = 0e1​=0 and e2=0e_2 = 0e2​=0, and the sum of the squares of its roots is 02−2(0)=00^2 - 2(0) = 002−2(0)=0, comfortably not negative. Yet for every real xxx we have x4≥0x^4 \ge 0x4≥0, so

    x4+1≥1>0x^4 + 1 \ge 1 > 0x4+1≥1>0

    and not one of its four roots is real. The reverse reading is false, and not by a narrow margin: the test passes while every single root fails to be real.

    So the implication runs one way only. A negative sum of squares proves that not all the roots are real, and no sign of that quantity ever proves that they are. That asymmetry is typical of what symmetric information can do. A total that no list of real numbers could have produced settles the matter outright, while a total that a real list could have produced settles nothing, because the very same total can be met in more ways than one.

    In one line

    For 2x4−4x3+9x2+5x−32x^4 - 4x^3 + 9x^2 + 5x - 32x4−4x3+9x2+5x−3 the two symmetric sums are e1=2e_1 = 2e1​=2 and e2=92e_2 = \frac{9}{2}e2​=29​, and e2e_2e2​ is the sum of six products of two different entries of the root list, never a sum of squares. Squaring e1e_1e1​ produces the four squares plus each mixed product twice, so r12+r22+r32+r42=e12−2e2=4−9=−5r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2 + r_4^2 = e_1^2 - 2e_2 = 4 - 9 = -5r12​+r22​+r32​+r42​=e12​−2e2​=4−9=−5, a negative number where e2e_2e2​ is positive. Since a real square is never negative, the four roots cannot all be real, and since the coefficients are real the non-real ones come in conjugate pairs, so at least two of the four are non-real. The reverse reading fails: x4+1x^4 + 1x4+1 has e1=e2=0e_1 = e_2 = 0e1​=e2​=0, so its sum of squares is 000, and yet x4+1≥1x^4 + 1 \ge 1x4+1≥1 for every real xxx, so none of its roots is real.

    Rubric

    Mark your own paper against this. Give yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down, not the ones you meant to.

    Part A 3 points

    2

    Divides both coefficients by the leading coefficient and attaches the right sign to each value. . Worth 2 points.

    1

    Writes the six terms out and describes a single term as a product of two different entries of the root list. . Worth 1 point.

    Part B 5 points

    2

    Squares the sum of the roots by taking one entry from each copy, and separates the same-entry choices from the mixed ones. . Worth 2 points.

    2

    Accounts for the factor of two by saying that each mixed product is drawn in two orders, rather than asserting it. . Worth 2 points. needs an explanation, not just an answer

    1

    Substitutes the two symmetric sums correctly and reports the value alongside e2e_2e2​ for comparison. . Worth 1 point.

    Part C 6 points

    3

    Settles the first question by an appeal to what a sum of squares of real numbers can be, stated so it can be checked without any root. . Worth 3 points. needs an explanation, not just an answer

    1

    Uses the conjugate pairing forced by real coefficients to say how many of the roots the conclusion reaches, without claiming more than the argument gives. . Worth 1 point.

    2

    Try a similar problem (Optional)

    Same idea, different numbers. Work it on paper, then check yourself the same way.

    For 3x3−3x2+12x−53x^3 - 3x^2 + 12x - 53x3−3x2+12x−5, find r12+r22+r32r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2r12​+r22​+r32​ and say what its value settles about the three roots.

    The answer

    r12+r22+r32=1−8=−7r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2 = 1 - 8 = -7r12​+r22​+r32​=1−8=−7. A negative total rules out three real roots, and since the coefficients are real the non-real ones come in a conjugate pair, so exactly two of the three roots are non-real and one is real.

    Read the two symmetric sums off the coefficients, dividing by the leading 333 each time:

    e1=−−33=1,e2=123=4e_1 = -\frac{-3}{3} = 1, \qquad e_2 = \frac{12}{3} = 4e1​=−3−3​=1,e2​=312​=4

    Then use the identity, which holds at any degree:

    r12+r22+r32=e12−2e2=1−8=−7r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2 = e_1^2 - 2e_2 = 1 - 8 = -7r12​+r22​+r32​=e12​−2e2​=1−8=−7

    A sum of squares of real numbers cannot be negative, so the three roots are not all real. More can be said, because the coefficients are real: non-real roots then arrive in conjugate pairs, so the number of non-real roots among the three is even, and it is not zero. It is therefore two, leaving exactly one real root.

    None of that required finding a root, and the value −7-7−7 is exact rather than an estimate.
